claim: TRPV1 channels in sensory neurons are integrators of painful stimuli and heat.
source: TRPV1 channels in sensory neurons are integrators of painful stimuli and heat, yet how they integrate diverse stimuli and sense temperature remains elusive.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that establishes the known function of TRPV1 channels, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: External sodium ions stabilize the TRPV1 channel in a closed state.
source: Here, we show that external sodium ions stabilize the TRPV1 channel in a closed state, such that removing the external ion leads to channel activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Removing external sodium ions leads to TRPV1 channel activation.
source: Here, we show that external sodium ions stabilize the TRPV1 channel in a closed state, such that removing the external ion leads to channel activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The temperature sensors in TRPV1 activate in two steps to favor opening.
source: In studying the underlying mechanism, we find that the temperature sensors in TRPV1 activate in two steps to favor opening, and that the binding of sodium to an extracellular site exerts allosteric control over temperature-sensor activation and opening of the pore.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the study supported by experimental data and modeling.

claim: The binding of sodium to an extracellular site exerts allosteric control over temperature-sensor activation and opening of the pore.
source: In studying the underlying mechanism, we find that the temperature sensors in TRPV1 activate in two steps to favor opening, and that the binding of sodium to an extracellular site exerts allosteric control over temperature-sensor activation and opening of the pore.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding supported by experimental data and allosteric modeling.

claim: The binding of a tarantula toxin to the external pore exerts control over temperature-sensor activation.
source: The binding of a tarantula toxin to the external pore also exerts control over temperature-sensor activation, whereas binding of vanilloids influences temperature-sensitivity by largely affecting the open/closed equilibrium.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data with DkTx shown in the manuscript.

claim: Binding of vanilloids influences temperature-sensitivity by largely affecting the open/closed equilibrium.
source: The binding of a tarantula toxin to the external pore also exerts control over temperature-sensor activation, whereas binding of vanilloids influences temperature-sensitivity by largely affecting the open/closed equilibrium.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data with capsaicin and modeling.

claim: TRP channels belong to a large and diverse superfamily of tetrameric cation channels that contain six transmembrane helices per subunit.
source: Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels belong to a large and diverse superfamily of tetrameric cation channels that contain six transmembrane helices per subunit (Liao et al., 2013; Hellmich and Gaudet, 2014), similar to voltage-activated ion channels (Long et al., 2007), ryanodine receptors (Yan et al., 2015) and IP3 receptors (Fan et al., 2015) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Several TRP channels are exquisitely temperature-dependent, enabling them to serve as biological thermosensors throughout the animal kingdom.
source: Several TRP channels are exquisitely temperature-dependent, enabling them to serve as biological thermosensors throughout the animal kingdom (Vay et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TRPV1 channel is a weakly voltage-dependent and cation-selective channel.
source: The vanilloid-sensitive TRPV1 channel is a weakly voltage-dependent and cation-selective channel that is expressed in nociceptive sensory neurons, where it acts as a sensor for noxious stimuli (Caterina and Julius, 2001) including heat, extracellular acidic pH, vanilloid compounds (e.g capsaicin), and venom toxins (e.g. double-knot toxin or DkTx) (see [Hilton et al., 2015] for review).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TRPV1 is expressed in nociceptive sensory neurons.
source: The vanilloid-sensitive TRPV1 channel is a weakly voltage-dependent and cation-selective channel that is expressed in nociceptive sensory neurons, where it acts as a sensor for noxious stimuli (Caterina and Julius, 2001) including heat, extracellular acidic pH, vanilloid compounds (e.g capsaicin), and venom toxins (e.g. double-knot toxin or DkTx) (see [Hilton et al., 2015] for review).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TRPV1 acts as a sensor for noxious stimuli including heat, extracellular acidic pH, vanilloid compounds, and venom toxins.
source: The vanilloid-sensitive TRPV1 channel is a weakly voltage-dependent and cation-selective channel that is expressed in nociceptive sensory neurons, where it acts as a sensor for noxious stimuli (Caterina and Julius, 2001) including heat, extracellular acidic pH, vanilloid compounds (e.g capsaicin), and venom toxins (e.g. double-knot toxin or DkTx) (see [Hilton et al., 2015] for review).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Protons can sensitize TRPV1 to activation by heat.
source: For example, protons can sensitize the channel to activation by heat (Jordt et al., 2000) and capsaicin (Jordt et al., 2000; Ryu et al., 2003), and both capsaicin (Voets et al., 2004; Matta and Ahern, 2007; Gregorio-Teruel et al., 2014) and protons (Lee and Zheng, 2015) can sensitize the channel to activation by voltage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Protons can sensitize TRPV1 to activation by capsaicin.
source: For example, protons can sensitize the channel to activation by heat (Jordt et al., 2000) and capsaicin (Jordt et al., 2000; Ryu et al., 2003), and both capsaicin (Voets et al., 2004; Matta and Ahern, 2007; Gregorio-Teruel et al., 2014) and protons (Lee and Zheng, 2015) can sensitize the channel to activation by voltage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Capsaicin can sensitize TRPV1 to activation by voltage.
source: For example, protons can sensitize the channel to activation by heat (Jordt et al., 2000) and capsaicin (Jordt et al., 2000; Ryu et al., 2003), and both capsaicin (Voets et al., 2004; Matta and Ahern, 2007; Gregorio-Teruel et al., 2014) and protons (Lee and Zheng, 2015) can sensitize the channel to activation by voltage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Protons can sensitize TRPV1 to activation by voltage.
source: For example, protons can sensitize the channel to activation by heat (Jordt et al., 2000) and capsaicin (Jordt et al., 2000; Ryu et al., 2003), and both capsaicin (Voets et al., 2004; Matta and Ahern, 2007; Gregorio-Teruel et al., 2014) and protons (Lee and Zheng, 2015) can sensitize the channel to activation by voltage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Allosteric models can explain how distinct stimulus-sensing domains are coupled to each other and to an internal gate within the pore.
source: Conceptually, these observations can be explained by allosteric models wherein distinct stimulus-sensing domains are coupled to each other (Latorre et al., 2007), and to an internal gate within the pore that opens and closes the ion permeation pathway (Salazar et al., 2009; Cao et al., 2013) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on allosteric models.

claim: Exchanging external Na+ with NMDG+ produces a rapid and reversible increase in outward currents at positive voltages at room temperature.
source: At room temperature, this simple manipulation produced a rapid and reversible increase in outward currents at positive voltages (Figure 1B), consistent with previous results (Ohta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and cited previous work.

claim: Application of saturating capsaicin further increases outward currents independently of whether external Na+ or NMDG+ is present.
source: Subsequent application of a saturating concentration of capsaicin further increased the outward currents independently of whether external Na+ or NMDG+ was present (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TRPV1 has a relatively low permeability to large cations like NMDG+.
source: At moderate TRPV1 expression levels, where outward Na+ currents could be accurately measured, the inward currents with external NMDG+ were negligible even in the presence of capsaicin (Figure 1B), indicating that TRPV1 has a relatively low permeability to large cations.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Exchanging external Na+ with NMDG+ produces variable and irreversible rundown of TRPV1 that increases with time in Na+-free solutions.
source: Although large outward currents induced by exchanging external ions were observed in all cells in which capsaicin evoked measurable currents, this manipulation also produced a variable and irreversible rundown of the channel that increased with time in Na+-free solutions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Exchanging external Na+ with NMDG+ produces large outward currents in human, mouse and chicken TRPV1 orthologues.
source: Exchanging external Na+ with NMDG+ also produced large outward currents in human, mouse and chicken TRPV1 orthologues (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which together with the previous report on porcine TRPV1 (Ohta et al., 2008), suggest that this phenomenon is a conserved feature of TRPV1 channels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and cited previous work.

claim: The phenomenon of Na+ regulation is a conserved feature of TRPV1 channels.
source: Exchanging external Na+ with NMDG+ also produced large outward currents in human, mouse and chicken TRPV1 orthologues (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which together with the previous report on porcine TRPV1 (Ohta et al., 2008), suggest that this phenomenon is a conserved feature of TRPV1 channels.
evidence: This is inferred from data across multiple species and cited previous work.

claim: I-V relations for fully activated TRPV1 channels in the presence of external Na+ or NMDG+ superimpose at positive voltages.
source: I-V relations for fully activated channels (10 µM capsaicin) in the presence of external Na+ or NMDG+ superimpose at positive voltages (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the unitary conductance of TRPV1 channels is similar under these conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The unitary conductance of TRPV1 channels is similar in the presence of external Na+ or NMDG+.
source: I-V relations for fully activated channels (10 µM capsaicin) in the presence of external Na+ or NMDG+ superimpose at positive voltages (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the unitary conductance of TRPV1 channels is similar under these conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Exchanging external solutions does not affect the single-channel current amplitude at positive voltages.
source: In addition, theoretical I-V relations calculated from the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation predict little change in unitary conductance at positive voltages (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), and we confirmed that exchanging external solutions does not affect the single-channel current amplitude (i) at positive voltages in outside-out patches containing a few channels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and theoretical calculations.

claim: Exchanging external Na+ with NMDG+ leads to spontaneous opening of the TRPV1 channel at room temperature.
source: From these results, we conclude that exchanging external Na+ with NMDG+ leads to spontaneous opening of the TRPV1 channel at room temperature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: NMDG+ does not activate TRPV1 in the presence of Na+.
source: This result indicates that NMDG+ does not activate the channel in the presence of Na+, but rather removal of external Na+ leads to channel activation.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Removal of external Na+ leads to TRPV1 channel activation.
source: This result indicates that NMDG+ does not activate the channel in the presence of Na+, but rather removal of external Na+ leads to channel activation.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Removal of internal Na+ produces no TRPV1 channel activation.
source: Removal of internal Na+ in recordings using inside-out patches produced no channel activation (Figure 2C, left panel), whereas removing external Na+ using outside-out patches led to robust activation (Figure 2C, right panel), demonstrating that the inhibitory influence of Na+ is limited to the external side of the TRPV1 channel.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The inhibitory influence of Na+ is limited to the external side of the TRPV1 channel.
source: Removal of internal Na+ in recordings using inside-out patches produced no channel activation (Figure 2C, left panel), whereas removing external Na+ using outside-out patches led to robust activation (Figure 2C, right panel), demonstrating that the inhibitory influence of Na+ is limited to the external side of the TRPV1 channel.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: External Na+ inhibition has an extrapolated apparent affinity (K1/2) at 0 mV of 2 mM.
source: We also measured the concentration-dependence for external Na+ inhibition over a range of voltages (Figure 2D) and found that inhibition was only weakly voltage-dependent, with an extrapolated apparent affinity (K1/2) at 0 mV of 2 mM (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: External Na+ inhibition is only weakly voltage-dependent.
source: We also measured the concentration-dependence for external Na+ inhibition over a range of voltages (Figure 2D) and found that inhibition was only weakly voltage-dependent, with an extrapolated apparent affinity (K1/2) at 0 mV of 2 mM (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: External Na+ stabilizes a closed state of the TRPV1 channel by binding to a site on the extracellular side of the protein.
source: These results suggest that external Na+ stabilizes a closed state of the TRPV1 channel by binding to a site on the extracellular side of the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experimental observations.

claim: The Na+ binding site is not highly selective for Na+, as external K+ can stabilize the closed state almost as effectively as Na+, followed by Rb+, Tris+, Cs+ and Li+.
source: This ion-binding site is not highly selective for Na+, as external K+ can stabilize the closed state almost as effectively as Na+, followed by Rb+, Tris+, Cs+ and Li+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changing external pH from 7.4 to 6 produces a pronounced shift in the concentration-dependence for Na+ inhibition to higher Na+ concentrations.
source: To explore a possible mechanistic link between the external Na+ site and acid regulation, we changed external pH from 7.4 to 6 and observed a pronounced shift in the concentration-dependence for Na+ inhibition to higher Na+ concentrations (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Activation of TRPV1 by pH 6 can be completely overcome by raising the Na+ concentration to 300 mM.
source: Moreover, activation of the channel by pH 6 could be completely overcome by raising the Na+ concentration to 300 mM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Protonation of acidic residues forming the Na+ binding site would lower the affinity of the metal ion.
source: These results are consistent with the expectation that protonation of acidic residues forming the Na+ binding site would lower the affinity of the metal ion, suggesting that the inhibitory Na+ binding site is intimately involved in the regulation of the TRPV1 channel by acid.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and knowledge of ion binding sites.

claim: Acidic solutions further stimulate TRPV1 channel activation in the absence of external Na+.
source: However, acidic solutions further stimulated channel activation in the absence of external Na+ (Figure 3A), indicating that protons also activate TRPV1 channels through a Na+-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Protons activate TRPV1 channels through a Na+-independent mechanism.
source: However, acidic solutions further stimulated channel activation in the absence of external Na+ (Figure 3A), indicating that protons also activate TRPV1 channels through a Na+-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Proton-mediated channel activation and proton-dependent potentiation of responses to other stimuli have distinct mechanisms.
source: These findings support the idea that proton-mediated channel activation and proton-dependent potentiation of responses to other stimuli have distinct mechanisms (Jordt et al., 2000; Ryu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Removal of external Na+ activates TRPV1 to a similar extent as a saturating concentration of DkTx.
source: Interestingly, removal of external Na+ before application of the toxin activates TRPV1 to a similar extent when compared with a saturating concentration of DkTx (Figure 3B and C), and removal of external Na+ did not produce further activation of DkTx-bound channels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Removal of external Na+ does not produce further activation of DkTx-bound TRPV1 channels.
source: Interestingly, removal of external Na+ before application of the toxin activates TRPV1 to a similar extent when compared with a saturating concentration of DkTx (Figure 3B and C), and removal of external Na+ did not produce further activation of DkTx-bound channels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Application of saturating capsaicin produces further activation of TRPV1 beyond that produced by DkTx or removal of external Na+.
source: In contrast, application of a saturating concentration of capsaicin produced further activation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: DkTx and external Na+ modulate TRPV1 through convergent mechanisms.
source: The lack of additivity for the activation of TRPV1 by DkTx and the removal of external Na+ contrasts with our results with acidic extracellular pH in the absence of external Na+ (Figure 3A), and suggests that DkTx and external Na+ modulate the TRPV1 through convergent mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3A, 3B, and 3C.

claim: E600 is involved in the inhibition of TRPV1 by external Na+.
source: A glutamate at position 600 near the top of S5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) has been previously associated with the inhibition of TRPV1 by external Na+ (Ohta et al., 2008), and has also been shown to be involved in the proton-dependent potentiation of TRPV1 responses to heat and capsaicin (Jordt et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: E600 is involved in the proton-dependent potentiation of TRPV1 responses to heat and capsaicin.
source: A glutamate at position 600 near the top of S5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) has been previously associated with the inhibition of TRPV1 by external Na+ (Ohta et al., 2008), and has also been shown to be involved in the proton-dependent potentiation of TRPV1 responses to heat and capsaicin (Jordt et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Removal of external Na+ no longer produces constitutive activation in E600Q mutant TRPV1 channels.
source: To confirm a key role of this residue in modulation of TRPV1 by external Na+, we investigated the effect of removing external Na+ on E600Q mutant channels, and found that the removal of external Na+ no longer produced constitutive activation even though the mutant remained responsive to capsaicin (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: E600Q mutant TRPV1 channels are not responsive to a saturating concentration of DkTx.
source: Consistent with DkTx and external Na+ having convergent mechanisms for modulating TRPV1, E600Q channels were not responsive to a concentration of DkTx that is saturating in WT channels (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: E600 is important for mediating channel inhibition by external Na+ and activation by DkTx.
source: These results demonstrate an important role for E600 in mediating channel inhibition by external Na+ and activation by DkTx, and suggest that this residue may be a part of the Na+ binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data with the E600Q mutant.

claim: E600 may be part of the Na+ binding site.
source: These results demonstrate an important role for E600 in mediating channel inhibition by external Na+ and activation by DkTx, and suggest that this residue may be a part of the Na+ binding site.
evidence: This is speculated based on experimental data with the E600Q mutant.

claim: Removal of external Na+ produces robust TRPV1 channel activation at depolarized potentials in channels lacking the pore turret.
source: Initially, we found that the removal of external Na+ produced robust channel activation at depolarized potentials in channels lacking the pore turret (Figure 3E), and that the addition of 10 µM capsaicin in the presence of external Na+ further activated the channels, similar to WT TRPV1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The removal of the pore turret increases the apparent affinity of TRPV1 for Na+.
source: Interestingly, the removal of the pore turret increased the apparent affinity of the channel for Na+ (Figure 3F), indicating that the pore turret does not form the Na+ binding site, but influences the cation-binding site through an allosteric mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The pore turret does not form the Na+ binding site.
source: Interestingly, the removal of the pore turret increased the apparent affinity of the channel for Na+ (Figure 3F), indicating that the pore turret does not form the Na+ binding site, but influences the cation-binding site through an allosteric mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The pore turret influences the cation-binding site through an allosteric mechanism.
source: Interestingly, the removal of the pore turret increased the apparent affinity of the channel for Na+ (Figure 3F), indicating that the pore turret does not form the Na+ binding site, but influences the cation-binding site through an allosteric mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Capsaicin is a partial agonist for the TRPV1 Δ604–626 construct.
source: Increasing the concentration of capsaicin from 10 to 40 µM did not further activate Δ604–626 TRPV1 channels in the presence of external Na+ (Figure 3E), indicating that 10 µM is a saturating concentration and that capsaicin is a partial agonist for this construct.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The pore turret is mechanistically associated with the modulation of TRPV1 by stimuli acting on the extracellular pore and by capsaicin.
source: This reveals that the pore turret is mechanistically associated with the modulation of the channel not only by stimuli acting on the extracellular pore (e.g. external Na+), but also by capsaicin that binds near the intracellular part of the protein (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data with the turret deletion construct.

claim: Mg2+ ions can activate the TRPV1 channel directly.
source: Contrary to what we observed for NMDG+, Mg2+ ions produced robust activation of the TRPV1 channel in the presence of 130 mM external Na+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), indicating that Mg2+ can activate the TRPV1 channel directly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TRPV1 is activated by noxious heat above 35°C in the absence of other stimuli.
source: TRPV1 is widely agreed to be activated by noxious heat above 35°C in the absence of other stimuli (Liu et al., 2003; Yao et al., 2010), but whether the channel responds to lower temperatures has not been carefully examined because the open probability (Po) in this temperature range is very low (Oseguera et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TRPV1 exhibits steep temperature-dependent activation over the entire temperature range explored (8°C to 45°C) in the presence of external Na+.
source: We measured macroscopic current-temperature (I-T) relations between ~8°C and 45°C using slow temperature ramps and observed steep temperature-dependent activation over the entire range of temperatures explored (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: TRPV1 exhibits steep temperature-dependence to Po at temperatures > 35°C at positive membrane voltages.
source: At temperatures > 35°C, we observed steep temperature-dependence to Po at positive membrane voltages (Figure 4C and D), which became even steeper at negative membrane voltages (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and E), consistent with previous studies (Voets et al., 2004; Yao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D and citations to previous work.

claim: TRPV1 exhibits steep temperature-dependence to Po at temperatures between 8 and 25°C.
source: At temperatures between 8 and 25°C, a range in which the temperature-sensitivity of TRPV1 has not been previously investigated, we also observed steep temperature-dependence to Po (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The entire Po-T relationship for TRPV1 cannot be described by a single temperature-dependent transition due to the presence of an apparent plateau near 22°C.
source: However, the entire Po-T relationship could not be described by a single temperature-dependent transition due to the presence of an apparent plateau near 22°C, raising the possibility that multiple temperature-dependent transitions are involved in the gating mechanism of TRPV1.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Multiple temperature-dependent transitions are involved in the gating mechanism of TRPV1.
source: However, the entire Po-T relationship could not be described by a single temperature-dependent transition due to the presence of an apparent plateau near 22°C, raising the possibility that multiple temperature-dependent transitions are involved in the gating mechanism of TRPV1.
evidence: This is speculated based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: I-T and Po-T relations in the absence of external Na+ display greatly diminished slopes compared to those in the presence of external Na+.
source: Remarkably, both I-T and Po-T relations displayed greatly diminished slopes and readily detectable channel activity at the lowest experimentally accessible temperatures (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Removal of external Na+ produces marked temperature-dependent inactivation of TRPV1 channels between 25 and 38°C.
source: In addition, removal of external Na+ produced marked temperature-dependent inactivation of TRPV1 channels between 25 and 38°C (Figure 5B, see yellow arrow), a process that typically occurs after repetitive cycles of heating and cooling in the presence of extracellular Na+ (Joseph et al., 2013) and at temperatures above ~50°C in single heat-activation experiments (Figure 5B, see purple arrow).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and citations to previous work.

claim: Temperature-inactivated TRPV1 channels can be partially responsive to saturating capsaicin.
source: Notably, temperature-inactivated channels could not be subsequently activated by heating, but were partially responsive to saturating capsaicin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) (Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and a citation to previous work.

claim: Capsaicin diminishes rundown of TRPV1 at room temperature when external Na+ is removed.
source: We also observed that capsaicin diminishes rundown at room temperature when external Na+ was removed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), consistent with a mechanistic link between temperature-dependent inactivation and channel rundown in the absence of external Na+ at room temperature.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Capsazepine causes a rightward shift in the Po-T relation of TRPV1 in the absence of external Na+, making the temperature-sensitive transition more readily detectable.
source: Indeed, the addition of capsazepine resulted in clear temperature-dependence of Po at low temperatures in the absence of external Na+ (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: Intermediate external Na+ concentrations produce clear temperature-dependence of Po at lower temperatures.
source: We obtained Po-T relations at 10, 30 and 65 mM external Na+, and observed clear temperature-dependence at low temperatures (Figure 6B), with enthalpies close to those measured in the presence of 130 mM external Na+ in the same temperature range (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: TRPV1 undergoes the same conformational transitions in response to heat regardless of whether external Na+ is present.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the TRPV1 channel undergoes the same conformational transitions in response to heat regardless of whether external Na+ is present, and thus that the enthalpy (ΔHo) associated with Na+ binding is not itself responsible for temperature-dependent gating (for a more detailed discussion see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 6A, B, and C.

claim: External Na+ modifies the midpoint (or entropy, △S) of the temperature-sensitive transition that operates at low temperatures.
source: Rather, it seems that external Na+ modifies the midpoint (or entropy, △S) of the temperature-sensitive transition that operates at low temperatures.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and modeling.

claim: External Na+ stabilizes a closed state of TRPV1 independently of its effect on temperature-sensitivity.
source: Additionally, external Na+ appears to stabilize a closed state of the channel independently of its effect on temperature-sensitivity, as the Po values corresponding to the inferred plateau regions (denoted by dotted lines in Figure 6B - insert) decrease as the concentration of external Na+ is increased.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Capsaicin has a larger effect on the closed/open transition of TRPV1 compared to the temperature-dependent transition.
source: Although we observed detectable temperature-dependent changes in Po at low temperatures for subsaturating concentrations of capsaicin, the Po values varied by more than 100-fold over the range of capsaicin concentrations, suggesting that capsaicin has a larger effect on the closed/open transition compared to the temperature-dependent transition (Figure 8A - insert).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The Po-T relation in saturating capsaicin exhibits marginal temperature-dependent changes.
source: The Po-T relation in saturating capsaicin exhibited marginal temperature-dependent changes, consistent with a large influence of capsaicin on the open/closed equilibrium of the channel leading to full receptor activation at a saturating concentration of this agonist (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: TRPV1 channels lacking the pore turret can be robustly activated by heat.
source: Interestingly, we found that the turret deletion can still be robustly activated by heat, albeit at somewhat higher temperatures compared to the WT channel (Figure 9A), confirming that the turret is not the temperature sensor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The pore turret is not the temperature sensor in TRPV1.
source: Interestingly, we found that the turret deletion can still be robustly activated by heat, albeit at somewhat higher temperatures compared to the WT channel (Figure 9A), confirming that the turret is not the temperature sensor.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Lowering temperature from 22 to 8°C decreases the efficacy of capsaicin in the turret-deletion TRPV1 construct.
source: At 8°C, the fractional activation by saturating capsaicin in the presence of external Na+ was substantially lower than what we observed at 22°C, revealing that lowering temperature further decreased the efficacy of capsaicin (Figure 9B; 8°C colored circles; 22°C colored ramps; see black arrows).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The turret deletion TRPV1 construct exhibits large temperature-dependent changes in Po in the presence of external Na+ and capsaicin, with two components separated by a clear plateau at intermediate temperatures.
source: We then obtained the full Po-T relationship in the presence of external Na+ and capsaicin, as before for the WT channel, but for the turret deletion we observed large temperature-dependent changes in Po, with two components in the relation separated by a clear plateau at intermediate temperatures (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B for Po-T relations from individual cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Capsaicin influences both the activity of the temperature-sensor and the open/closed equilibrium of TRPV1, but has a larger influence on the latter.
source: Together, these results qualitatively show that capsaicin influences both the activity of the temperature-sensor and the open/closed equilibrium, but appears to have a larger influence on the latter.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data with the turret deletion construct.

claim: Activation of TRPV1 by heat is effectively ablated between 5 and 35°C in the presence of external Na+ and DkTx.
source: We therefore measured Po-T relations in the presence of external Na+ and DkTx to test whether the binding of the toxin has an effect on temperature-sensitivity, and observed that activation of the channel by heat was effectively ablated between 5 and 35°C (Figure 10, and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B for Po-T relations from individual cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: DkTx exerts strong control over temperature-sensor activation in TRPV1.
source: These results demonstrate that DkTx also exerts strong control over temperature-sensor activation, which in our model can be achieved simply by trapping the channel in the intermediate plateau and preventing temperature-sensor deactivation or full activation (Figure 10, insert).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 10 and modeling.

claim: TRPV1 has evolved external Na+ binding sites that must be occupied for the channel to remain closed at physiological body temperatures in mammals.
source: First, our results demonstrate that the TRPV1 channel has evolved external Na+ binding sites that must be occupied for the channel to remain closed at physiological body temperatures in mammals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Without external Na+, TRPV1 would be spontaneously open at physiological temperatures, many channels would be inactivated, and responses to noxious heat would be diminished.
source: The steeply temperature-sensitive transition that normally opens TRPV1 in response to noxious heat still operates in the absence of Na+, yet without external Na+ the channel would be spontaneously open at physiological temperatures, many channels would be inactivated, and responses to noxious heat would therefore be diminished.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and reasoning about physiological implications.

claim: The Na+ regulatory mechanism plays a fundamental role in tuning the properties of TRPV1 to serve as a detector of noxious heat and acid.
source: Thus, this Na+ regulatory mechanism plays a fundamental role in tuning the properties of TRPV1 to serve as a detector of noxious heat and acid, and possibly other stimuli that have yet to be examined.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and their physiological implications.

claim: The role of the first temperature-sensitive transition in TRPV1 is to maintain the channel in a closed state at physiological temperatures.
source: Our results suggest that the role of the first temperature-sensitive transition is to maintain the channel in a closed state at physiological temperatures, whereas the second transition functions to activate the channel in response to noxious heat.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and modeling.

claim: The second temperature-sensitive transition in TRPV1 functions to activate the channel in response to noxious heat.
source: Our results suggest that the role of the first temperature-sensitive transition is to maintain the channel in a closed state at physiological temperatures, whereas the second transition functions to activate the channel in response to noxious heat.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and modeling.

claim: External Na+ exerts strong control over the first temperature-sensitive transition in TRPV1.
source: It is interesting that both Na+ and capsaicin do not seem to have a substantial impact on the second transition, at least to the extent that we could study this component in the presence of inactivation. In contrast, external Na+ exerts strong control over the first transition.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and modeling.

claim: Capsaicin has a larger influence on the open/closed equilibrium of TRPV1 than on the temperature-sensing machinery.
source: These observations suggest that the vanilloid has a larger influence on the open/closed equilibrium than on the temperature-sensing machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data.

claim: The existence of multiple temperature-sensitive transitions in TRPV1 provides a possible explanation for why Po-T relations at negative voltages are at least two-fold steeper than at positive voltages.
source: The existence of multiple temperature-sensitive transitions also provides a possible explanation for why Po-T relations at negative voltages are at least two-fold steeper than at positive voltages (Figure 4B) (Voets et al., 2004; Yao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculated based on experimental data and modeling.

claim: The Na+ binding sites in TRPV1 are likely located outside the ion permeation pathway within each subunit.
source: Because Na+ inhibition has only very weak voltage-dependence, these Na+ binding sites are likely to be located outside the ion permeation pathway within each subunit.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing weak voltage-dependence.

claim: E600 is an excellent candidate for forming the Na+ binding site in TRPV1.
source: E600 in the extracellular loop just after the S5 helix (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) has been proposed to be responsible for proton-mediated potentiation of heat- and capsaicin-dependent activation of the channel (Jordt et al., 2000), making it an excellent candidate for forming the Na+ binding site.
evidence: This is speculated based on previous work and experimental data.

claim: The structural changes in the external pore observed in the RTx/DkTx-bound TRPV1 structure are tightly associated with the temperature-sensing machinery.
source: The present findings with external Na+ and DkTx suggest that these structural changes in the external pore are tightly associated with the temperature-sensing machinery, either by participating in allosteric coupling or in the actual mechanism of temperature-sensing.
evidence: This is speculated based on experimental findings and structural data.
